results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Bringer of the Last Gift, Superior Spider-Man and Town Greeter.
results.text:
This is a Sultai graveyard brew (black-green-blue), and the deck was accepted.

**The plan:** Town Greeter, Molt Tender, Cache Grab, Dredger's Insight and Overlord of the Balemurk mill cards from your own library into the graveyard. Bitter Triumph and Dreadwing Scavenger let you discard a Bringer that gets stuck in your hand. Once a Bringer is in the graveyard, you cast Superior Spider-Man (turn 4, or turn 3 with Llanowar Elves) and have him enter as a copy of Bringer.

You cast Spider-Man, so Bringer's "if you cast it" ability still triggers. Every other creature is sacrificed, which wipes the opponent's board. Then every creature card that was already in a graveyard comes back. Extra Bringers return as 6/6 fliers and Overlords as 5/5s. A returning Overlord's enter ability mills four more cards and gets a creature back to your hand, often the next Spider-Man. Late in the game, Elves and Molt Tender can also give you enough mana to cast Bringer from your hand for its full 8.

**Directions I considered:**
1. Sultai, borrowing the Golgari Roots self-mill package (Molt Tender, Cache Grab, Dredger's Insight, Overlord) and adding blue for Spider-Man. **This is the one I chose.**
2. Dimir Midrange's looters and removal with green added for Town Greeter.
3. A ramp deck that casts Bringer from hand.

I picked the first because Golgari Roots is the only proven shell that already runs Town Greeter. It also mills creatures fast enough to turn on Spider-Man by turn 4. The mana borrows from Roots, plus blue dual lands and Starting Town.

**Things to know:**
- **Odds:** With only 4 Spider-Men (he's legendary), you'll have one by turn 4 on the play about 53% of the time. You'll almost always have a mill or discard card by then (99.7%). Cache Grab, Dredger's Insight and Overlord can also pull a milled Spider-Man back into your hand. The checker reported 2.7% for drawing all five cards in my listed line by turn 6. That number is misleading: the core combo only needs Spider-Man in hand and a Bringer in the graveyard.
- **The opponent gets creatures back too.** Bringer returns all creature cards from *every* graveyard, including theirs. Against aggro decks with creatures in their graveyard, cast it when your graveyard is clearly bigger than theirs.
- **Your own creatures are lost.** Your creatures on the battlefield (Elves, Tender, Greeter) get sacrificed, and Bringer's wording keeps them from coming back that same turn. It works best when you have a light board and a full graveyard.

The sideboard has hand disruption and counterspells against Vivi Cauldron and Azorius Control, artifact and enchantment answers (Disruptive Stormbrood, Scrapshooter), Ghost Vacuum for opposing graveyards, and extra removal for Izzet Aggro.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Mightform Harmonizer, Spell Snare and Full Bore.
results.text:
I couldn't include Spell Snare: the card database says it's **not legal in Standard**, so no Standard deck can play it. I built the deck around Mightform Harmonizer and Full Bore as a Gruul (red-green) landfall brew, where "landfall" means abilities that trigger whenever a land enters. Snakeskin Veil takes over the job Spell Snare would have done: protecting your creature for one mana on the turn you go for the kill. No published list plays these cards together, so this is untested.

**The plan:** Harmonizer doubles one creature's power every time a land enters. Full Bore adds +3 power first, so there's more to double. On turn 4, a typical line is:
1. Cast Full Bore on Tifa Lockhart, taking her from 1 to 4 power.
2. Play Fabled Passage. Tifa's own landfall ability and Harmonizer's both double her: 4 → 16.
3. Sacrifice the Passage to fetch a basic land. That's a second landfall: 16 → 64 power with trample.

Traveling Chocobo makes each land trigger happen an extra time, so even a plain basic land is enough. Full Bore on a Harmonizer cast for its cheaper warp cost (3 mana instead of 4) also gives it trample and haste. That gives you a surprise 14+ power hitter even if your board was just cleared.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Gruul built on the Landfall deck from the format menu (chosen).** It uses that deck's creatures (Tifa, the Chocobos, Bristly Bill, Mossborn Hydra) and its fetch lands. It's the strongest choice because those cards already multiply landfall triggers, which is exactly what Harmonizer and Full Bore reward.
2. **Temur (adding blue) with Spell Pierce as a stand-in for Spell Snare.** I passed because a third color makes the mana worse in a deck that needs green early and red for Full Bore.
3. **A red aggro build like Boros Aggro, splashing green for Harmonizer.** Full Bore shows up in those lists, but they don't have the land-trigger engine that makes Harmonizer worth playing.

**Honest odds:** In an 11-card look (turn 5 on the play), you have about a 57% chance to draw at least one Harmonizer. The chance of having Harmonizer, Full Bore and a good creature to pump all together is about 26%. The full turn-4 line with every named card lands well under 1% of the time, so treat it as the ceiling. In practice the deck usually wins through repeated landfall growth from Mossborn Hydra, Bristly Bill and Sazh's Chocobo, with Harmonizer and Full Bore as the finishers.

**Mana:** 25 lands, matching the Landfall decks (about 24.8 on average). The deck has 16 red sources for Full Bore and 25 green sources.

**Sideboard:** It's aimed at the top decks in the format: removal against Izzet and Boros Aggro, Magebane Lizard against Vivi Cauldron and control, and artifact/enchantment and graveyard answers against Cauldron and Reanimator.

--- Lands ---
Lands changed after the build: 2 Forest out, 1 Commercial District, 1 Starting Town in. The deck had 11 basic lands; Standard two-color decks from the last 90 days (2195 lists) average 8.9, and the lands that came in are the ones they fix their colors with.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Airbender Ascension, Bramble Familiar and Appa, Steadfast Guardian.
results.text:
This is a Bant (white-blue-green) brew. It's built on a loop of exiling your own permanents and recasting them cheaply ("airbending"). The only real list running all three of your cards was a five-color "Rogue" deck. From it I took Doc Aurlock and Aang, Swift Savior. From the Simic Ouroboroid deck on the menu I took the Llanowar Elves ramp and the green-blue lands.

**The plan:** Ramp out with Llanowar Elves and Bramble Familiar, then flash in Appa at the end of your opponent's turn and exile Bramble Familiar (plus Quantum Riddler, Outcaster Trailblazer and so on). Airbended cards can be recast for {2}, and Doc Aurlock makes that free. So Bramble's 7-mana Adventure, Fetch Quest, costs nothing: it mills seven and puts a creature, enchantment or land from them onto the battlefield. Every spell you cast from exile also makes Appa create a 1/1 Ally token. Those tokens and recasts add counters to Airbender Ascension, and once it has four it re-enters Appa at each of your end steps. That restarts the loop every turn. You win when Fetch Quest finds Craterhoof Behemoth, or you cast it off your mana creatures, and it pumps the token army for lethal around turn 6.

**Directions I considered:**
1. A Selesnya (green-white) version using the menu's Selesnya Offense creature package.
2. A Boros-style white Ally deck.
3. Bant built around Doc Aurlock.

I picked Bant because Doc Aurlock turns every airbend recast, including Fetch Quest, from {2} into {0}. Neither of the other directions could do that.

**Outcaster Trailblazer:** The checker pointed out that few players run it. I kept it because recasting it for free with Doc still adds a mana, so each Appa or Ascension cycle gains you mana. Plotting it costs only {G} with Doc, and casting it from exile later triggers Appa again.

**Things to know:**
- **One rules assumption:** I'm assuming the airbend {2} cost lets you cast Bramble's Adventure side (Fetch Quest), and that the Familiar then stays in exile, so you can cast it from there later. That fits how I understand Adventures, but my tools couldn't confirm it.
- **Realistic odds:** You'll have Appa, Bramble or Doc, and Ascension all together by turn 5 in about 24% of games. The submit tool put drawing every card in the full win line by turn 6 at just 1.3%, because it requires a Craterhoof in hand. You don't need one, since Fetch Quest can find it, and a partial engine still makes plenty of Ally tokens and extra cards.
- **The mana stretches across three colors:** 22 lands with 13 white, 13 blue and 18 green sources, plus 7 mana creatures (11 counting Trailblazer). Simic Ouroboroid decks run about 21 green sources, so you'll sometimes stumble on Appa's {W}{W} or Craterhoof's {G}{G}{G}.

The 15-card sideboard covers the main meta decks:
- **Aggro:** Seam Rip and Dragon Sniper.
- **Vivi Cauldron and Reanimator:** Keen-Eyed Curator and Tishana's Tidebinder.
- **Control:** Negate and Disdainful Stroke.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Abandon Attachments, Firebending Lesson and Combustion Technique.
results.text:
I built an Izzet Lessons Tempo deck. It's a brew, and the submitted list was accepted as legal.

**Three directions I considered:**
1. **Mono-Red firebending.** This is the only real list running all three cards: one Mono-Red deck that placed 13th at the Standard Challenge on 2025-11-20.
2. **Izzet Lessons tempo.** It uses the red cards from Izzet Aggro on the menu (Hired Claw, Burst Lightning, and its red/blue lands) plus blue creatures that get better with Lessons in your graveyard.
3. **Red-green Uncle Iroh / Toph value.** A slower deck that makes Lessons cheaper and gets extra value from them.

**I chose Izzet.** Abandon Attachments costs {1}{U/R}, so blue fits it naturally. Blue also adds creatures that grow from your graveyard: First-Time Flyer, Sokka, and Dragonfly Swarm. That gives all three of your cards more to do than they would in mono-red.

**The plan:** Play cheap creatures on turns 1–2 (Hired Claw, Fire Nation Cadets, Firebending Student, First-Time Flyer). Firebending Lesson clears a blocker for one mana. Abandon Attachments trades spare lands or Lessons for fresh cards, which also puts more Lessons in your graveyard. That pile is what turns on Cadets' firebending and the Flyer's +1/+1. It also grows Dragonfly Swarm, whose power equals the noncreature spells in your graveyard. And it powers Combustion Technique, which deals 2 damage plus one per Lesson in your graveyard and exiles the creature, so by midgame it removes the biggest blocker for 2 mana. The fliers and prowess creatures should win around turn 6.

**Things to know:**
- **Lesson count:** The deck runs 14 Lessons, and Thundering Falls can also drop one from the top of your library into the graveyard. You'll have at least one Lesson by turn 3 in 92.5% of games. You'll have drawn Combustion Technique by turn 3 in about 49%.
- **The winning line isn't fixed:** The checker said a game draws every card in my example line by turn 6 only 0.7% of the time. The deck doesn't need that exact sequence; each step has several cards that can do the same job.
- **Lands:** I run 22. Izzet Aggro lists average about 24, but this deck's average mana cost is 1.71 and the checker suggested about 21.6. Abandon Attachments also lets you discard extra lands.
- **The menu's Izzet Aggro list is outdated:** Screaming Nemesis is now banned, so I left it out. Vivi Ornitier is banned too, so the Vivi Cauldron numbers on the menu may not reflect today's field.
- **Sokka:** I run only 3 because he's legendary and you can only control one at a time.
- **Sideboard:** Fire Magic and Abrade are for go-wide decks and artifacts. Soul-Guide Lantern is for graveyard decks. It'll Quench Ya! and Magebane Lizard are for control.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Ashling, Rekindled, Sunderflock and Bounce Off.
results.text:
I built **Izzet Elemental Ramp**, a brew. The deck plays nothing but Elementals and ramps into Sunderflock on turn 4. When Sunderflock is cast, it returns every non-Elemental creature to its owner's hand. Here, that means only the opponent's creatures get bounced, and then your 5/5 flier and the rest of your board attack.

**How the three cards fit together**
- **Ashling, Rekindled:** On turn 3 you pay {U} to transform it. The other side adds 2 mana every turn that can only be spent on spells costing 4 or more, so it ramps straight into Sunderflock and Ashling's Command. Since Ashling is a 2-mana Elemental, Sunderflock also costs 2 less.
- **Sunderflock:** Its cost goes down by the highest mana value among your Elementals. It costs 7 with Ashling out, 5 with Twinflame Travelers, and 3 with Ice Flan. Flamebraider taps for 2 mana that can only go to Elemental spells, which Sunderflock is. So on turn 4, Ashling + Flamebraider + 4 lands is enough to cast it.
- **Bounce Off:** Besides being a cheap tempo spell, it can return your own Sunderflock to your hand for {U}. That saves it from removal, or lets you cast it again to bounce the opponent's board a second time. Sunderflock only bounces when it's cast, which is why getting it back to your hand matters.

**Directions I considered**
1. **The Dimir "Incarnation" reanimator shell** (Deceit, Wistfulness, Not Dead After All). It's the only kind of published deck that has run Sunderflock, but it has no red, so Ashling doesn't fit.
2. **The Izzet Aggro spell package** (lots of burn and cheap spells) to power Eddymurk Crab, a 7-mana Elemental that gets cheaper with spells in your graveyard. It's strong, but it pulls the deck away from Ashling's ramp.
3. **An all-Elemental Izzet ramp deck that borrows the Izzet Aggro mana base and Burst Lightning.** I chose this one because both of the deck's ramp sources pay for Sunderflock directly.

**Odds to know**
- By turn 4 (on the play, no mulligans), you have about a 79% chance of drawing Ashling or Flamebraider.
- The chance of also having Sunderflock or Eclipsed Flamekin (which digs for Elementals) is about 61%.
- The submission tool reported that the full listed line, with every named card drawn by turn 7, comes together in only about 5% of games. That's because the line names five different cards. You don't need all of them: the core is Ashling or Flamebraider plus Sunderflock.

The mana (24 lands, 15 blue and 15 red sources) passed the deck check against real Izzet Aggro lists. The sideboard is aimed at the current top decks: counterspells for control and Lessons, Pyroclasm for aggro, Sunspine Lynx, and Soul-Guide Lantern for Reanimator.

--- Lands ---
Lands changed after the build: 3 Island, 3 Mountain out, 2 Multiversal Passage, 4 Steam Vents in. The deck had 14 basic lands; Standard two-color decks from the last 90 days (2523 lists) average 8.2, and the lands that came in are the ones they fix their colors with.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Insatiable Avarice, Doomsday Excruciator and Archenemy's Charm.
results.text:
I built **Mono-Black Demons**, a Standard brew. It's a grindy midrange deck that cuts both players down to six cards and then makes the opponent run out of cards first.

**The plan:** Doomsday Excruciator exiles all but the bottom six cards of each player's library. After that, Insatiable Avarice's {B}{B} mode, aimed at the opponent, makes them draw three of their last few cards and lose 3 life. They run out of cards before you do, unless the 6/6 flier, Unholy Annex and Bloodletter of Aclazotz have already killed them.

- **Annex and Bloodletter:** Unholy Annex drains 2 each turn while you control a Demon. Demon Wall, Bloodletter and Excruciator are all Demons. Bloodletter doubles any life the opponent loses on your turn, so Annex drains 4 and Avarice costs them 6.
- **Avarice's other job:** before Excruciator lands, its {2} mode finds Excruciator for you.
- **Archenemy's Charm:** it's removal (exiles a creature), protection (pumps with lifelink) and recursion (brings a dead Excruciator or Bloodletter back to hand).

**Three directions I considered:**
1. A Dimir draw-go version using Stock Up and Three Steps Ahead.
2. A pure deck-out version.
3. A mono-black Demons version using the cheap interaction from Dimir Midrange on the menu (Deep-Cavern Bat, Cecil, Shoot the Sheriff, Bitter Triumph).

I chose the third. Excruciator costs six black mana, so the deck needs 24 black-producing lands, which only mono-black allows. It also gives Annex Demons from turn 2 and keeps the deck-out plan as a finisher, not the whole deck. The mana follows the 13 Mono-Black lists I compared against: 24 lands (21 Swamp, 3 Realm of Koh). I left out the colorless Soulstone Sanctuary because it doesn't help cast Excruciator.

**How likely the plan is:**
- **Finding Excruciator:** with 3 Excruciator plus 4 Avarice to tutor for it, you have 7 ways to find it. You'll see at least one of them by turn 5 77.8% of the time.
- **Drawing everything:** naturally drawing every piece of the full line by turn 8 happens only about 6% of the time. That number ignores Avarice's tutoring, Annex's extra cards and Charm's recursion, so the real figure is higher. Still, most games you win by grinding with Bloodletter and Annex, and the deck-out is the finisher.
- **Your own clock:** once Excruciator resolves, you draw 2 cards a turn, so you also have only about three turns left. Count both libraries before you cast it, and use Avarice on the opponent quickly.

**The sideboard** is aimed at the current field:
- Deathmark and Day of Black Sun against the green decks (Ouroboroid, Landfall, Aang).
- Duress against Jeskai Control and Lessons.
- Strategic Betrayal against Reanimator.
- Stab and Nowhere to Run against Izzet and Boros aggro.
- The End.

No published list in the last 400 days plays these three cards together, so this is a new build. It borrows the fast-mana core from Mono-Red Prison (Ancient Tomb, City of Traitors, Simian Spirit Guide). Prison is 5% of the current field.

**The plan:** You never pay for Apex Devastator (10 mana) or Call Forth the Tempest (8). Creative Technique and Tibalt's Trickery each reveal cards until they hit a nonland card, then cast it for free. The deck runs 37 lands and only 23 spells, so those reveals usually land on Apex, Call Forth or another Technique.

**Main line:** Ancient Tomb + Mountain + Spirit Guide + Lotus Petal casts Technique on turn 2.
- Copying Technique (its demonstrate ability) gives you two reveals. The opponent also gets a copy, so skip copying when their free spell would hurt you.
- Apex's four cascades chain into more free spells.
- Call Forth then deals 15+ damage to each of the opponent's creatures. That clears blockers, and a 10/10 Apex finishes the game around turn 4.

**Backup line:** Cast Lotus Petal and counter it with your own Trickery. Petal's name is skipped, so you cast the next real spell for free, as early as turn 1 (Mountain + Spirit Guide).

**Why this direction:** I considered three:
- **Show and Tell into Omniscience**, borrowed from Sneak and Show. Sneak Attack and Show and Tell put creatures onto the battlefield without casting them, so Apex's cascade never triggers. Omniscience works, but then your three cards are just extras next to a stronger combo.
- **Green ramp to hardcast Apex.** Far too slow for Legacy.
- **A lands-heavy red deck where Technique and Trickery are the engine.** I chose this one because it's the only version where all three of your cards are the actual plan.

**Things to know:**
- **Land count:** The checker warned that 37 lands is about 15 more than normal. That's on purpose: every spell you add makes a reveal more likely to whiff.
- **Speed odds:** Without mulligans, you have Technique or Trickery by turn 2 on the play 70.6% of the time, and by turn 3 on the draw 79%. Seeing a cheat card plus fast mana by turn 2 is 64.8%. The draw lands (Sunbaked Canyon, Fiery Islet) and cycling lands raise these a bit.
- **Checker statistic:** The tool reported that all the line's cards are drawn by turn 4 in only 0.1% of games. That's because the line lists both routes (Technique and Trickery) and every possible hit, and you only need one route.
- **Weaknesses:** Apex and Call Forth are dead cards in your hand. Apex has no haste or trample, so Swords to Plowshares and Force of Will are real problems. That's why the sideboard has Pyroblast to counter blue spells, plus Defense Grid.

--- Lands ---
Lands changed after the build: 10 Mountain out, 4 Taiga, 4 Wooded Foothills, 2 Commercial District in. The deck had 16 basic lands; Legacy two-color decks from the last 90 days (1182 lists) average 2.2, and the lands that came in are the ones they fix their colors with.

results.prompt: Brew me a Legacy deck built around Arclight Phoenix, Buried Alive and Flow State.
results.text:
I built a Grixis (blue-black-red) Arclight Phoenix combo deck. It's a brew: no published list in the last 400 days runs these three cards together. Arclight Phoenix and Buried Alive appear together in just one Modern list.

**The plan:** Buried Alive is a 3-mana sorcery that puts up to three creatures from your library into your graveyard. Here it puts in three Arclight Phoenixes. At the start of combat, each Phoenix returns from the graveyard if you've cast three or more instants and sorceries that turn, and they come back with haste.

- **Main line:** Dark Ritual (instant, turns one black mana into three) → Buried Alive → Flow State. Flow State is a 2-mana sorcery that normally keeps 1 of your top 3 cards. With an instant and a sorcery already in your graveyard it keeps 2 instead, so it refills your hand while counting as the third spell. All three Phoenixes then return and hit for 9 flying damage.
- **Turn-1 kill:** Badlands or Underground Sea → Dark Ritual → Buried Alive → Gut Shot (paid with 2 life) is a 9-damage turn 1.
- **Later turns:** The Phoenixes come back on any turn you cast three cheap spells. Faithless Looting is a second way to get them into the graveyard by discarding them.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Ritual combo (chosen):** Borrows the fast-mana package from the Oops All Spells, Doomsday and Epic Storm lists in your meta summary: Dark Ritual, Lotus Petal and Manamorphose (which pays for itself and draws a card). I picked it because Buried Alive costs 3 mana, and these cards let you cast it and still hit three spells on turns 1–3.
2. **Izzet/Dimir Tempo shell:** Phoenix as a recurring threat behind Daze and Force of Will. Buried Alive does very little in that shell.
3. **Reanimator hybrid:** Buried Alive also finds Griselbrand for Reanimate. That splits the deck between two plans.

**Odds and risks:**
- You see Buried Alive or Faithless Looting by turn 2 on the play about 71% of the time, before counting any card draw.
- Buried Alive plus Dark Ritual or Lotus Petal by turn 2 is about 30%. Brainstorm, Ponder and Flow State are there to raise that.
- The checker gave only 0.8% for drawing every card in the listed line by turn 3. That number is misleading: it requires every named card, including the fourth one (Lava Dart) and the Phoenixes, which Buried Alive tutors for. Assembling it in practice is far more likely than that.
- **Your worst matchups** are graveyard hate (Surgical Extraction) and Consign to Memory, which counters the Phoenixes' return trigger.

**Card choices worth knowing:**
- I kept 1 Gut Shot even though almost no Legacy deck plays it. Paying 2 life makes it a free third spell, and its target (the opponent) is always legal.
- I went to 15 lands. The checker suggested about 14, and Epic Storm lists run about 12.5, but Lava Dart's flashback needs lands to sacrifice. Lava Dart counts toward the three spells twice, once from hand and once from the graveyard.
- The sideboard (Pyroblast, Surgical Extraction, Thoughtseize, Pyrokinesis, Kolaghan's Command, Toxic Deluge, Fatal Push) is aimed at the tempo decks, the combo decks and Tron. Several of those cards are cheap instants that also count toward the three spells.

results.prompt: Brew me a Vintage deck built around Goblin Welder, Legion Extruder and Sewer-veillance Cam.
results.text:
I submitted a Vintage brew built around Goblin Welder, Sewer-veillance Cam and Legion Extruder, labeled as a brew.

**How the deck wins.** The three cards you named make an infinite combo. You need Welder on the battlefield, Cam on the battlefield and Extruder in the graveyard:
1. Tap Welder to sacrifice Cam and return Extruder. Cam leaving the battlefield untaps Welder, and Extruder entering deals 2 damage.
2. Tap Welder again to sacrifice Extruder and return Cam. Cam entering untaps Welder.
3. Repeat. Each loop deals 2 damage, with no limit.

**How it finds the pieces.** Goblin Engineer and Melded Moxite put Extruder (or Cam) straight into the graveyard. The Moxen, Lotus and artifact lands give Welder and Engineer artifacts to sacrifice. The backup kill is Painter's Servant plus Grindstone, which mills the opponent's whole library. Painter set to blue also makes Pyroblast hit any spell or permanent, and turns every card in your hand blue so Force of Will can exile anything.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Chosen: blue-red Welder combo.** This takes the shell from Legacy "Sewer Combo", the only real deck that runs all three of your cards (2 recent Legacy lists). On top of that it adds the Moxen, Force of Will, Ancestral/Time Walk and Urza's Saga package from the Lurrus PO decks in the menu.
2. **Workshop prison** using the Sphere Shops package. Mishra's Workshop can't help cast Welder, and Sphere effects tax your own cheap spells.
3. **Mono-red Ancient Tomb Welder.** Without blue mana you can't cast Cam, which breaks the infinite loop.

I picked the first because it keeps your three cards as the main kill and adds the strongest interaction Vintage has.

**Notes:**
- **Odds:** The draw odds tool gives about a 21% chance of naturally drawing Welder, Cam and Extruder-or-Engineer together by turn 4 on the draw. That figure ignores card draw, the Painter backup kill and mulligans. Ancestral, Brainstorm, Moxite and Engineer's tutor push the real number higher, but this is a combo deck that has to dig for its pieces.
- **Melded Moxite:** The checker flagged it as rarely played in Vintage. I kept it because its discard puts a combo piece into the graveyard, and Vexing Bauble or Gitaxian Probe can't do that.
- **Mana:** 15 lands, close to Lurrus PO's average of about 14.5. Blue sources are 13 against Lurrus PO's 16.6, which is enough because only Cam and a few spells need blue. Red sources are 15.
- **Sideboard:** It targets the menu decks: graveyard hate for Dredge, Mindbreak Trap for the storm-style decks, artifact removal for Shops, and Ensnaring Bridge and Sudden Demise for creature decks.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pauper deck built around Ardent Recruit, Search Party Captain and Springleaf Drum.
results.text:
I built **Boros Metalcraft Soldiers**, a brew on the Boros Synthesizer artifact shell. No published list from the last 400 days plays Ardent Recruit, Search Party Captain and Springleaf Drum together, so nobody has tested this combination yet.

**The plan:** Play cheap creatures and cheap artifacts on turns 1–2, so Ardent Recruit gets +2/+2 from having three artifacts out (Recruit's "metalcraft" ability). By turn 3 the Clue from Thraben Inspector, artifact lands and Drum usually do that. Then attack with everything and cast Search Party Captain after combat. It costs {1} less for each creature that attacked, so it often costs just {1}{W} and draws a card. Springleaf Drum has three jobs:
- **Artifact count:** it's a one-mana artifact toward the three Recruit needs.
- **Mana:** creatures you just played can still be tapped for Drum, so it fast-starts a two-spell turn.
- **Repeat value:** it's a cheap artifact for Glint Hawk to return to your hand (instead of sacrificing the Hawk) and for Kor Skyfisher to bounce, then you replay it.

Lightning Bolt and Galvanic Blast (4 damage when you have three artifacts) clear blockers or finish the game around turn 5–6.

**Three directions I considered:**
1. **Mono-White go-wide**, using the Mono-White Aggro package from the meta list (Inspectors, Battle Screech, Prismatic Strands). It has lots of attackers for Captain, but too few artifacts for Recruit, and Battle Screech's flashback taps the same creatures Drum wants.
2. **Orzhov Glintblade** (Glint Hawk, Cast Down, Lembas). It's a good artifact base, but more controlling and slower than a one-drop Recruit wants.
3. **Boros Synthesizer shell (chosen):** it has the most artifacts (24 counting Clue-makers), Glint Hawk and Kor Skyfisher to reuse Drum, and two burn spells that run on the same three-artifact count as Recruit. Every piece supports the three cards you asked for.

**Notes:**
- I run 18 lands, while real Synthesizer lists average about 20.5. The checker flagged this. I kept 18 because the deck's average mana value is 1.48 (no Lembas or Melded Moxite) and the four Drums also make mana.
- With 4 copies of each named card, you'll see a Recruit or a Drum by turn 3 only about 49% of the time. The plan doesn't depend on them alone: 23 cards make or count as artifacts and 20 creatures can attack for Captain.
- The sideboard targets the current meta: Red Elemental Blast for Terror and Faeries, Dust to Dust for Affinity, Electrickery for Elves and white swarms, Relic of Progenitus for graveyard decks.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pauper deck built around Aurora Eidolon, Sandstorm Eidolon and Spirit Mascot.
results.text:
I built a Boros (red-white) multicolor aggro deck. The idea: the two Eidolons come back from your graveyard whenever you cast a multicolored spell, and every card that leaves your graveyard puts a +1/+1 counter on Spirit Mascot.

**What each requested card does here:**
- **Sandstorm Eidolon:** Pay {R} and sacrifice it, and target creature can't block this turn. That clears the way for your attack.
- **Aurora Eidolon:** Pay {W} and sacrifice it to prevent 3 damage to any target. That saves a creature from burn or a bad block.
- **Getting them back:** After you sacrifice either Eidolon, your next multicolored spell returns it to your hand. The deck has 22 multicolored spells, because red/white hybrid cards count: Boros Recruit, Battlegate Mimic, Fire at Will, plus gold cards like Stonebound Mentor, Skyknight Legionnaire, Pursue the Past and Mascot itself.
- **Spirit Mascot:** It gets a +1/+1 counter whenever one or more cards leave your graveyard. Its 17 triggers are the Eidolons coming back plus flashback spells (Firebolt, Rally the Peasants, Prismatic Strands, Pursue the Past).
- **Stonebound Mentor:** A 3/3 for three that scries 1 off the same graveyard triggers.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Boros multicolor creatures with flashback cards (chosen).**
2. **The Mono-White Aggro / Boros Aggro package** (Battle Screech, Prismatic Strands, Rally the Peasants). It has too few multicolored spells to bring the Eidolons back.
3. **The Mono-Red Rally shell built on Burning-Tree Emissary.** It has almost nothing white to make Aurora Eidolon or Mascot worth playing.

I picked the first because every creature also returns an Eidolon. I did borrow the flashback cards (Rally the Peasants, Prismatic Strands) from the second, and the mana base from the existing Boros Aggro lists. My 19 lands give 15 white and 13 red sources, close to theirs.

**How it wins:** Play cheap first-strikers and Mascot on turns 1–3, and use Bolt and Firebolt to remove blockers. From turn 4, sacrifice Sandstorm Eidolon to stop a blocker, then cast a multicolored creature to get the Eidolon back (and grow Mascot). Battlegate Mimic also becomes a 4/2 first striker for the turn when you do this. Finish with Rally the Peasants (+2/+0 to your team), then flash it back for more damage and another Mascot counter. A typical kill is around turn 6.

**Honest odds:**
- You'll see at least one Eidolon by turn 5 about 72% of the time.
- You'll have a multicolored spell to bring it back almost every game (99.6%).
- The exact six-card example line comes together only about 1.6% of the time. The deck is built so that any Eidolon plus any multicolored spell runs the same loop.
- No published list has played these three cards together, so this is untested.

The 15-card sideboard is aimed at the current top decks: Red Elemental Blast and Pyroblast for blue decks like Terror, Electrickery for go-wide decks, Dust to Dust for artifact decks, extra Prismatic Strands against the burn-heavy red decks, and Journey to Nowhere and Thraben Charm for big creatures.

--- Lands ---
Lands changed after the build: 1 Plains out, 1 Sacred Peaks in. The deck had 10 basic lands; Pauper two-color decks from the last 90 days (968 lists) average 9.0, and the lands that came in are the ones they fix their colors with.

results.prompt: Brew me a Premodern deck built around Living Death.
results.text:
I built a black-green **Living Death brew**. Living Death acts as your mass reanimation spell and a board wipe at the same time.

**How it wins:** Load your graveyard with huge creatures, then cast Living Death. It sacrifices everything on the battlefield, including all of your opponent's creatures, and then returns every creature card from your graveyard at once. The best line is turn 2 Dark Ritual into Buried Alive, which puts Akroma, Symbiotic Wurm and Visara from your deck into your graveyard. On turn 3 or 4, Living Death (5 mana) comes off a Ritual or Birds of Paradise. Akroma has haste and protection from red and black, so she attacks right away. Visara taps to kill any new blocker. Symbiotic Wurm leaves seven 1/1s behind if it's removed, or if you sacrifice it to a second Living Death. That's about a turn-5 win.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Black reanimator:** Dark Ritual, Putrid Imp and Cabal Therapy with Living Death on top. Fast, but it mostly turns back into the existing Reanimator deck.
2. **Hermit Druid self-mill:** Hermit Druid puts your deck into the graveyard, then Living Death brings it all back. The problem is that Hermit Druid also mills the Living Deaths themselves.
3. **Black-green Survival, rebuilt around Living Death (my pick):** Living Death shows up most in black-green Survival in real Premodern lists. I kept that deck's mana and its Birds/Survival core, then added the reanimator pieces (Dark Ritual, Putrid Imp, Cabal Therapy) and Buried Alive. I picked this because it has the most ways to fill the graveyard (13 cards). Also, Living Death works as a one-sided wrath against the creature decks in the field: Sligh, Goblins, Elves, Madness and Terravore.

**Things to know:**
- **Draw odds:** About 61% of the time you've seen a Living Death (or Insidious Dreams to set one on top) by turn 4. You've seen a graveyard filler 89% of the time.
- **The 0% the checker reported is misleading.** It counts games where you *draw* every card in the line by turn 5, but you never draw Akroma, Visara or the Wurm. Buried Alive and Survival put them in the graveyard. The deck's only white sources are 4 City of Brass/Gemstone Mine, but that's fine because you never cast Akroma or Phantom Nishoba from your hand.
- **Lands:** I ran 20 lands, below the 21–23 the checker suggests. The 7-mana-and-up creatures are never cast, so the deck's real curve is lower than it looks. Birds and Ritual add early mana.
- **Main weakness:** Living Death also returns your opponent's creatures from their graveyard, so watch for that against Hermit Druid or Reanimator. Graveyard removal like Tormod's Crypt is a real threat too, and it's very common in Sligh and Goblins lists. The sideboard includes Withered Wretch, plus Xantid Swarm and an extra Duress against the counterspell decks.
